sections.heading: 2. Implementation
sections.text: The DLCB compiler and runtime is organised into three stages, summarised in Figure 1 . The PyTorch-DLCB bridge (§ 2.1 ) intercepts a PyTorch program, partitions it into compilable regions, applies shape generalisation, and lowers each region to the DLCB IR. Graph compilation (§ 2.2 ) then takes the IR, builds a system of shape constraints incrementally as operators are added, runs optimisation passes (fusion, pattern-matching rewrites, and automatic stride assignment), partitions the graph into thunks, and produces two compilation artefacts per thunk: a CUDA kernel (or a call into a vendor library) generated by kgen (§ 2.2.3 ), and a compact host program generated by the host code generator (§ 2.2.4 ) that resolves dynamic dimensions at launch time. At inference time (§ 2.3 ), the DLCB runtime executes each thunk’s host program to compute kernel arguments and dispatches the corresponding kernel.

sections.heading: 2.1. PyTorch-DLCB bridge
sections.text: The PyTorch-DLCB bridge is the entry point through which PyTorch programs are lowered to DLCB. It operates on the PyTorch JIT intermediate representation and is responsible for partitioning the program into compilable regions, lowering each region to DLCB IR, applying shape generalization, and registering the compiled binaries as custom operators that are transparent to the rest of the PyTorch runtime.

sections.heading: 2.1.1. Subgraph identification.
sections.text: The bridge maintains a predicate over PyTorch JIT operator names that defines the supported subset : the operators that DLCB can compile. It walks the JIT graph in topological order, classifying each node as supported or unsupported. Consecutive supported nodes are merged into contiguous compilation regions ; unsupported nodes form boundaries between regions and are left in place to be executed natively by the PyTorch runtime. A node that consumes the output of an unsupported node contributes a region input; a supported node whose output is consumed by an unsupported node (or is a graph output) contributes a region output. The result is a partition of the JIT graph into an alternating sequence of DLCB-compiled regions and natively executed operators.

sections.heading: 2.1.2. Lowering to DLCB IR.
sections.text: For each compilation region the bridge extracts the subgraph and translates it operator-by-operator into a DLCB IR graph. Each tensor input to the region is registered with the DLCB compiler as either static or dynamic . In static mode, the concrete shape and stride values recorded during tracing are passed directly, allowing DLCB to treat every dimension as a compile-time constant. In dynamic mode, fresh symbolic dimension variables are allocated for both shape and strides, so the compiler treats every dimension as an unknown to be resolved at runtime by the constraint solver. Scalar and constant-tensor arguments are always lowered with their concrete values. Once lowered, the graph is compiled and the resulting binary is stored in a specialisation cache keyed on rank and element type (see § 2.3 ); subsequent invocations with the same rank reuse the cached binary without recompilation.

sections.heading: 2.1.3. Shape generalization.
sections.text: When a model is traced under static shapes, the bridge applies an automatic shape generalization pass before lowering. The pass takes the JIT IR and automatically identifies which dimensions are safe to abstract into free symbolic variables, producing a parameterized kernel that can be reused whenever the program is called with different concrete shapes, eliminating recompilation and removing the burden of manual shape annotation from the user. The pass proceeds in four steps.

sections.heading: Identifying shape consumers.
sections.text: A predicate determines which argument positions of which operators can safely receive a dynamic (symbolic) shape value. For example, the second argument of aten::reshape —the target shape list—is a shape consumer: replacing its concrete integer values with symbolic variables is safe because the operator is defined entirely by the shape it is given. The predicate covers all such argument positions across the supported operator set.

sections.heading: Tracing dim-computing subgraphs.
sections.text: For each shape-consuming use, the pass recursively walks the def-use chain of the shape argument to collect all nodes that compute it. Recognised node kinds are: • Leaf sources : aten::size and constant nodes. • List construction : list-construction nodes, whose inputs are themselves recursively traced. • Arithmetic on dims : aten::add , aten::sub , aten::rsub , aten::mul , aten::floordiv , and truncating aten::div . • Unary and coercion nodes : aten::neg and scalar coercion operations. The result is a topologically ordered list of nodes forming the shape-computation subgraph rooted at the consumer’s input.

sections.heading: Cloning and redirecting.
sections.text: The pass iterates over every node in the JIT block. For each shape-consuming use it collects the corresponding dimension-source cluster, clones every node in the cluster into fresh nodes inserted immediately before the consumer, and redirects the consumer’s input to the cloned output. Cloning is necessary because a shape-computing node—e.g. an aten::size call—may be shared between a static use and a shape-consuming use. After cloning, dead-code elimination removes the originals that are no longer needed, and the cloned dimension-computing nodes are pulled into the DLCB compilation group, where they are compiled symbolically.

sections.heading: Symbolic tensor inputs.
sections.text: When a tensor input to a compilation group is registered, the bridge checks whether it is static or dynamic. For a static input, concrete integer lists for the shape and strides are passed directly to the compiler. For a dynamic input, fresh symbolic dimension variables are allocated for both shape and strides, so that DLCB treats every dimension as an unknown. When the layout-preservation option is enabled, the strides are sorted to recover the memory layout order (e.g. row-major or channel-last), and this structural constraint is encoded alongside the symbolic dimensions, allowing DLCB to generate layout-aware kernels while keeping dimension sizes symbolic.

sections.heading: 2.1.4. Broadcast optimization.
sections.text: PyTorch traces record concrete shapes, which means the bridge knows—before any lowering occurs—which dimensions have size 1 in the traced execution and are therefore being broadcast. The bridge exploits this information as a broadcast hint : for each binary operator whose inputs differ in shape in the trace, the size-1 dimensions are annotated as statically broadcast. DLCB uses these annotations during code generation to emit specialised broadcast paths that avoid redundant index arithmetic for the broadcast dimension, producing more efficient kernels than would be possible if every dimension were treated as fully general. Because the hint is derived from the static trace rather than the dynamic inputs, it is validated at runtime: the host program includes a check that verifies the broadcast dimension is indeed 1 before dispatching the specialised kernel, falling back to the general path if the check fails.

sections.heading: 2.2. Graph compilation
sections.text: Once a subgraph has been extracted, operators are added to the DLCB IR graph one at a time. As each operator is added, it contributes equalities to a system of shape constraints that capture the relationships between tensor dimensions imposed by that operator: a pointwise binary operator asserts broadcast compatibility between its two inputs and equates the output shape to the broadcast result; a matrix multiplication constrains the inner dimensions of its operands to match and defines the output shape from the outer dimensions; a reshape operator equates the product of input dimensions to the product of output dimensions; and so on, covering reductions, gather/scatter, and other supported operation classes. Shape inference is run incrementally after each operator is added, propagating the new constraints through the solver immediately. This provides fail-fast behaviour: if an operator introduces a contradiction—for example, a shape mismatch between two operands—the error is detected at graph-construction time rather than after the full graph has been built, giving immediate feedback on the source of the error.

sections.heading: 2.2.1. Optimization Passes
sections.text: Once the graph is fully constructed, a series of optimization passes are applied before code generation. Automatic stride assignment initialises any tensor whose layout has not been explicitly specified to row-major order. Fusion passes merge compatible operator sequences, including pointwise fusion and folding transposes into adjacent matrix multiplications, reducing kernel launches and improving memory-access locality. Pattern-matching rewrites identify common operator subgraphs and substitute more efficient implementations; for example, the canonical layer normalisation subgraph—a mean subtraction followed by variance computation and division—is recognised and replaced by a single fused layernorm operator, eliminating redundant mean evaluations and enabling a hardware-optimised implementation.

sections.heading: 2.2.2. Partitioning
sections.text: After the optimization passes, the DLCB IR graph is partitioned into thunks . A thunk is a general-purpose compilation unit: it accepts a fixed set of tensor inputs, produces a fixed set of tensor results, and encapsulates all the computation needed to do so. The partitioner inspects each operator and groups operators into thunks according to how they will be compiled and executed. Library operators —principally matrix multiplications and convolutions—each form their own singleton thunk backed by a vendor-optimised library call. Matrix multiplications are dispatched to cuBLAS or cuBLASLt, and convolutions to cuDNN. The partitioner does not attempt to fuse these operators with their neighbours, since the vendor libraries apply their own internal optimisations. All remaining operators—pointwise and elementwise operations (unary and binary arithmetic, activations, type casts), reductions, and index transformations such as reshapes and transposes—are grouped into thunks backed by custom CUDA C++ kernels generated by kgen (§ 2.2.3 ). Consecutive such operators are merged into a single thunk wherever possible, allowing kgen to emit one fused kernel covering the entire sequence and eliminating intermediate memory traffic between operators.

sections.heading: 2.2.3. Kernel code generation (kgen)
sections.text: Given the fused operator graph and the dimension assignments produced by the constraint solver, kgen uses coordinate-based inference to determine, for each output element, which input coordinates are required. Starting from the set of output tensors and their coordinate spaces, kgen propagates coordinates backwards through each operator in topological order, building a map from output coordinates to the input coordinates and intermediate values needed to compute them. It then emits a CUDA kernel that iterates over output coordinates, evaluating this map to read inputs and write outputs. Dynamic dimension values—those left as free parameters by the constraint solver—appear in the generated kernel as integer parameters. The values of these arguments are computed at launch time by the host code interpreter described in § 2.2.4 , ensuring that a single compiled kernel binary executes correctly across any shapes for which the rank and layout structure match. More details of how kgen generates kernels parameterized by dynamic dimensions are described in § 4 .

sections.heading: 2.2.4. Host code generation
sections.text: After constraint solving, some dimension expressions remain unsolved: they depend on runtime values that are not yet known. The host code generator compiles these residual expressions into a compact interpreted program that runs on the CPU immediately before each kernel launch—i.e. before a given thunk is launched. It produces two artefacts: an instruction sequence and a context record (a table mapping tensor identifiers and operator ports to the host program’s input and output slots). Together they allow the kernel launcher to supply runtime shapes, verify shape constraints, compute derived dimensions, and pass the results to the kernel as launch arguments.

sections.heading: Input variable allocation.
sections.text: First, the generator scans all input tensors in the thunk. For each input tensor whose rank is statically known, it inspects every shape dimension. Dimensions already resolved to compile-time constants require no runtime value and are assigned no input slot. Each remaining non-literal shape dimension is assigned a sequential input variable index, and the mapping is stored in a per-tensor input table. The same variable index is then introduced into the constraint system as a named literal, effectively naming the runtime value of that dimension so that inference can propagate it through the constraint graph.

sections.heading: Output slot registration.
sections.text: The generator then constructs an ordered list of output expressions, one slot per non-literal dimension value that the kernel will need at launch time. Three categories of output are registered: • Tensor shapes and strides. For every input, output, and intermediate tensor with a known rank, each non-literal shape and stride dimension is assigned a sequential output slot. Statically resolved dimensions are assigned no slot. • Kernel generator constants. Some graph partitions are compiled to an opaque thunk—such as for cuDNN and cuBLAS ops. Such thunks may declare expressions for constants that need to be dynamically computed. Each is assigned an output slot so that it is computed by the host program. • Dynamic operator attributes. Operators that carry dimension-list attributes (e.g. reshape target shapes) expose those as outputs, one slot per attribute element.

sections.heading: Inference and stride promotion.
sections.text: With input variables named and output expressions registered, the generator re-runs the constraint solver on the combined constraint set which consists of the remaining constraints for the graph, plus all the constraints added by input variable allocation and output slot registration. If a stride output remains unsolved after inference—its expression still contains a free variable—the generator promotes that stride to an additional input variable. It inserts a new named-literal equality constraint equating the stride expression to the fresh input variable and re-runs inference. This handles operators whose output strides cannot be derived algebraically from shape information alone and must therefore be read from the tensor descriptor at launch time.

sections.heading: Program representation.
sections.text: The host program is a flat, ordered sequence of instructions executed by a simple register machine with three classes of storage: inputs (read-only integer values supplied at runtime), outputs (writeable slots read by the kernel launcher after execution), and registers (temporaries private to the program). The instruction set comprises sixteen opcodes: data movement ( CP , LD , ST , MOV ); arithmetic on two source registers ( ADD , SUB , MUL , DIV , DIV_CEILING , MOD , MIN , MAX ); BROADCAST , which applies the NumPy broadcasting rule and returns false on incompatible shapes; CHK_EQ , which compares two registers and returns false if they differ; and FASTINTOP_CONSTS , which writes the precomputed magic constants (M,s,n) for a divisor read from one source register.

sections.heading: Compilation.
sections.text: The host program compiler translates the ordered output list and the residual constraint set into the instruction sequence by recursive descent with memoisation. For each output slot the compiler inspects the expression rooted at that slot: • If the expression is a named literal (a direct alias for an input variable), it emits a single CP instruction. • Otherwise it recursively compiles the expression tree, which returns the register holding the computed value, and emits ST to write that register to the output slot. For each residual constraint whose both sides are fully resolved, the compiler compiles both sides and emits CHK_EQ . The recursive compilation dispatches on the expression kind: integer literals emit MOV ; named literals emit LD from the corresponding input slot; arithmetic expressions compile their operands and emit the matching instruction; and fast-integer-division constants compile the divisor and emit FASTINTOP_CONSTS , returning the register for the requested (M,s,n) component. Results are memoised by expression identity.

sections.heading: Storage and invocation.
sections.text: The compiled instruction sequence and the context record are stored as part of the thunk. At kernel launch time, the DLCB runtime fills the input vector from the concrete shapes and strides of the live input tensors via the context record, then runs the interpreter. The interpreter maintains a flat register file and dispatches each instruction in order via a switch statement; BROADCAST and CHK_EQ can return false early to signal an incompatible shape or violated constraint, while all other instructions are infallible. On success the output vector contains the resolved shapes, strides, and kernel constants, which are passed directly to the CUDA kernel as launch arguments. The host program is compiled once at graph compilation time and interpreted cheaply on every invocation, keeping symbolic computation off the inference critical path.

sections.heading: 2.3. Runtime kernel launch
sections.text: At inference time, pytorch-dlcb maintains a per-subgraph cache of compiled thunks. On each invocation it computes a specialisation key from the live input tensors—encoding element type, rank, and (in static mode) concrete shape and stride values, plus the full content of any constant tensor or scalar arguments—and looks up the key in the cache. On a hit the cached thunk is executed immediately. On a miss the DLCB compiler pipeline is invoked to compile the subgraph, a runtime context is created with bound cuBLAS, cuBLASLt and cuDNN handles, GPU buffers for embedded data constants are allocated and initialised, and the resulting thunk is inserted into the cache before execution. Three kinds of thunk are produced, depending on what was known about tensor shapes at compile time.

sections.heading: Static thunks.
sections.text: When all tensor shapes are fully known at trace time, the subgraph is compiled into a static thunk . The specialisation key includes the concrete shape and stride values of every input, so a distinct thunk exists for each combination of shapes encountered at runtime. The thunk contains fully static CUDA kernels whose launch configurations—grid dimensions, block dimensions, and shared memory size—are resolved entirely at compile time. At invocation the runtime proceeds directly to memory allocation and kernel dispatch; there is no host-side shape computation.

sections.heading: Dynamic (AOT) thunks.
sections.text: When tensor ranks are statically known but dimension sizes are not, the subgraph is compiled into a dynamic thunk . The specialisation key includes only rank and element type, so a single thunk handles all inputs with the same rank regardless of their concrete sizes. At invocation the runtime runs the thunk’s host program (§ 2.2.4 ) to resolve the dynamic dimensions, then proceeds as follows: (1) Shape registration. The concrete sizes and strides of each live input tensor are recorded. (2) Shape commitment. The host program interpreter is run, propagating the registered shapes through the compiled constraint program to resolve output shapes, strides, and other necessary constants. (3) Scratch space computation. Each thunk wrapper is queried for the temporary GPU memory it requires given the now-known shapes. (4) Memory allocation and kernel dispatch. A single temporary tensor pool is allocated. For each thunk wrapper, input tensors are mapped from the live PyTorch tensors, output tensors are allocated from the shapes produced by the host program, and intermediate tensors are sub-allocated from the pool and freed by reference counting as soon as their last consumer completes. Each wrapper is then dispatched with the resolved storage pointers and the current CUDA stream.

sections.heading: JIT thunks.
sections.text: When tensor rank is not statically known, the constraint solver cannot produce a parameterized kernel ahead of time. The subgraph is instead stored as a JIT thunk containing the uncompiled DLCB IR. On the first invocation with a given set of concrete shapes the IR is compiled on-demand, the resulting kernels are cached inside the thunk, and execution proceeds. Subsequent invocations with the same shapes bypass compilation entirely. From pytorch-dlcb’s perspective the JIT path is transparent: the same cache-lookup mechanism is used, and the outer specialisation cache avoids redundant compilation by keying on rank rather than concrete values.

sections.heading: 3. Constraint Solving
sections.text: Shape constraints are solved by a generic fixed-point inference engine parameterised over the graph representation it operates on. The engine is instantiated for two distinct purposes: solving dimension-size constraints (the dimlist inference described here) and solving coordinate-set constraints used during kernel code generation (§ 4.3 ).

sections.heading: Constraint representation.
sections.text: Every constraint is an equality between two dimension expressions , represented by nodes in a DAG. Six node kinds are used: • Integer literals — a concrete integer constant. • Named literals — a named constant whose numerical value is unknown at compile time but will be supplied at runtime (e.g. an input tensor’s batch dimension). Named literals are preserved by the solver and appear in the generated host program as inputs. • Free variables — unknowns to be eliminated by the solver. • Arithmetic expressions — a binary arithmetic expression with operator drawn from { add , sub , mul , div , div_ceiling , mod , min , max , scale , broadcast }. • Shape lists — an ordered list of dimension expressions, representing a full tensor shape. • List operations — a list operation with operator drawn from { append , broadcast }, used to express broadcast and concatenated-rank shapes. Each node tracks its set of free variables and a content-addressed hash, enabling O(1) structural equality tests. The constraint set is a list of equality pairs (l,r), cross-indexed by vertex so that all constraints mentioning a given node can be found in O(\log n). Reference counting on nodes supports prompt dead-code elimination when a node is no longer referenced by any constraint or graph root.

sections.heading: Fixed-point algorithm.
sections.text: The solver iterates over the constraint set, applying the first applicable rewrite rule at each step and restarting the scan whenever a rule fires, until no rule applies. The rules, in priority order, are: (1) Trivial equality. e=e\;\Rightarrow\;\varnothing. Remove the constraint and prune the vertex. (2) Variable substitution. x=e where x\notin\mathit{FV}(e)\;\Rightarrow\; substitute e for x everywhere in the graph, then erase the constraint. This is the primary elimination step: it removes the variable x from the problem entirely. (3) Constant conflict check. c_{1}=c_{2} where both sides are integer literals \;\Rightarrow\; fail if c_{1}\neq c_{2}. Contradictory constraints cause the solver to return failure. (4) Batch list substitution. [x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]=[c_{1},\ldots,c_{n}] where all x_{i} are variables and all c_{i} are literals \;\Rightarrow\; substitute each c_{i} for x_{i} simultaneously. This optimised rule avoids the overhead of unpacking the list into n separate constraints when the solution is immediate. (5) Reordering. e=x \;\Rightarrow\; flip to x=e. Variables are normalised to the left-hand side so that rule 2 can apply. (6) List unpacking. [x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]=[y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}]\;\Rightarrow\;x_{1}=y_{1},\;\ldots,\;x_{n}=y_{n}. A rank mismatch produces a failure. (7) Append unpacking. Two rules strip one element at a time from the trailing or leading end of an append expression equated with a concrete list, generating one scalar equality per element. For example, e_{1}\mathbin{@}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]=[y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}] produces [x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]=[y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}] and e_{1}=[\,]. (8) Arithmetic inversion. Three rules solve simple linear equations when one side is a concrete literal: \displaystyle e\cdot c_{1} \displaystyle=c_{2}\;\Rightarrow\;e=c_{2}/c_{1}\quad(\text{when }c_{1}\mid c_{2}), \displaystyle e+c_{1} \displaystyle=c_{2}\;\Rightarrow\;e=c_{2}-c_{1}, \displaystyle e-c_{1} \displaystyle=c_{2}\;\Rightarrow\;e=c_{1}+c_{2}. (9) Common-subexpression cancellation. (f\;a\;b)=(f\;a\;c)\;\Rightarrow\;b=c for additive and subtractive operators with a shared operand. (10) Partial-expression substitution. (f\;e_{1}\ldots e_{k})=c where the expression node has remaining uses in the graph \;\Rightarrow\; substitute c for the expression node throughout the graph while keeping the constraint alive. This propagates known values to all sites that compute the same sub-expression. After every substitution the graph is updated: affected ancestor nodes have their hashes and free-variable sets recomputed in topological order, and any node whose reference count drops to zero is pruned by a depth-first sweep.

sections.heading: Sufficiency in practice.
sections.text: Although the rule set does not handle arbitrary systems of equations, we have found it sufficient for all constraints arising from real-world programs. The key reason is that constraints are not generated arbitrarily: they are produced mechanically by a fixed set of supported operators, each of which contributes a small, well-understood family of equalities—broadcast compatibility, reshape products, matmul inner-dimension matching, and so on. The structural regularity of this constraint vocabulary means that the rules above cover every pattern that can actually appear. General-purpose constraint solvers (e.g. SMT-based approaches) would be capable of handling a much wider class of constraints but would impose unnecessary overhead and complexity; the bounded operator set makes them unnecessary.

sections.heading: Expression simplification.
sections.text: Before a node is used in a new constraint or substituted into the graph, it is passed through a simplification pass. Simplification performs constant folding for all arithmetic operations, and eliminates algebraic identities such as x+0\Rightarrow x, x\times 1\Rightarrow x, x/1\Rightarrow x, and \min(x,x)\Rightarrow x. Nodes are content-addressed, so structurally identical expressions are automatically deduplicated.

sections.heading: Outcome.
sections.text: After the solver reaches a fixed point, three kinds of dimension expression remain in the constraint graph: • An integer literal — the dimension is fully determined at compile time and can be hard-coded in the generated kernel. • A named literal — the dimension is a direct function of a runtime input (e.g. a linear expression of the input batch size). The named literal is recorded in the kernel parameter table as an argument to be supplied at launch time; statically resolved dimensions receive no entry. • A residual expression containing free variables — the dimension depends on shapes that cannot be determined even symbolically. Residual constraints are compiled by the host code generator (§ 2.2.4 ) into a lightweight interpreted program that evaluates them at kernel launch time.

sections.heading: 4.4. CUDA C++ Code Generation
sections.text: Once the coordinate map is complete, kgen generates a CUDA C++ kernel structured as follows. The generated CUDA C++ source is compiled to a binary using NVIDIA’s NVRTC runtime compilation library. The resulting cubin is extracted and stored in the thunk alongside the host program. NVRTC runs once at graph compile time; at inference time the cubin is loaded by the CUDA driver and launched without further compilation overhead.

sections.heading: Thread-to-coordinate mapping.
sections.text: The kernel is launched with a one- or two-dimensional thread grid that covers all positions in the output coordinate space. Each thread computes its output coordinate from blockIdx and threadIdx using the output tensor’s strides.

sections.heading: Dynamic dimension parameters.
sections.text: Any dimension value not resolved to a compile-time constant appears as an entry in a const int32_t* buffer passed to the kernel as a parameter. Each such value is loaded once at the start of the kernel into a local variable; all index arithmetic references the local variable. The host program (§ 2.2.4 ) fills this buffer before each launch.

sections.heading: Index arithmetic and memory access.
sections.text: For each input tensor the kernel evaluates the inferred coordinate expression to compute a flat memory index and loads the value. Scalar coordinate expressions are emitted as inline C++ arithmetic; vector coordinate spaces produce vectorised loads (e.g. float4 ) where alignment permits. Predicate conditions arising from boundary tiles or masked reductions are emitted as guards, substituting a default value (zero or the reduction identity) when the predicate is false.

sections.heading: Operator evaluation.
sections.text: Operators are emitted in topological order, reusing values shared across multiple consumers. Each operator maps to an inline C++ expression or intrinsic. The final result is written to the output tensor at the thread’s output coordinate.

sections.heading: 4.5. Dynamic Vectorization
sections.text: GPU memory bandwidth is best exploited when threads issue wide, aligned loads and stores using CUDA vector types such as float4 or half8 . For kernels with statically known shapes, the required conditions—that the last dimension is contiguous in memory and its size is divisible by the vector width—can be verified at compile time, so a single fixed-width kernel is emitted. Dynamic-shape kernels do not have this luxury: dimension sizes and memory strides are not known until the kernel is launched.

sections.heading: Compile-time width selection.
sections.text: kgen selects a candidate vector width v at compile time using two inputs: (i) the hard-coded maximum width of an 8-element wide vector, and (ii) the element type of the tensors involved, which constrains which CUDA vector types are valid (e.g. float32 only supports widths of 1, 2, and 4). If any operator in the DAG uses a type for which no vector load exists—such as complex types—the candidate width is reduced to 1 and a purely scalar kernel is emitted. Subject to these constraints, the code generator targets the largest width v that is valid.

sections.heading: Runtime guard.
sections.text: Because divisibility and contiguity cannot be established at compile time, the generated kernel contains both a vectorized branch and a scalar fallback branch, selected by a runtime boolean guard. kgen always attempts to vectorize the innermost (last) dimension. The guard evaluates two conditions against the dynamic dimension buffer loaded at kernel entry: (1) Divisibility : the last-dimension size of every input and output tensor is divisible by v. (2) Contiguity : the stride of the last dimension of every input and output tensor equals 1 (i.e. elements are contiguous in memory). If both conditions hold the vectorized branch executes; otherwise the scalar fallback (v=1) executes.

sections.heading: Coordinate grouping and code generation.
sections.text: When the vectorized branch is taken, kgen generates a kernel in which the thread count is divided by v: each thread is responsible for v consecutive elements along the vectorized dimension. After coordinate inference resolves the symbolic index map, the code generator identifies groups of v consecutive coordinate expressions—using the algebraic simplification rules of the constraint engine (§ 3 ) to establish consecutiveness—and merges each group into a single vector coordinate expression. These vector coordinates expressions are lowered to CUDA vector loads and stores, maximizing memory-access efficiency.

sections.heading: 5. Evaluation
sections.text: We evaluate DLCB on the Torchvision benchmark suite, which contains a wide range of image classification and segmentation models. All experiments are run on an NVIDIA H100 GPU with CUDA 13.2, cuDNN 9.20, and PyTorch 2.11. All models were run using half precision (fp16). Each model is run for 3 warmup iterations followed by 5 timed iterations.

sections.heading: 5.1. End-to-end inference throughput
sections.text: Figure 3 shows speedup over PyTorch eager on the TorchVision classification suite. Overall, the static mode achieves a 1.10x speedup and the dynamic mode 0.92x speedup relative to eager. Since this paper focuses on dynamic-shape compilation, we discuss the dynamic mode in more detail. Dynamic mode shares all optimisation passes with static mode, with several passes extended to handle symbolic shapes (e.g., the pattern matcher matches symbolic dimensions, and the kernel generator guards vectorised code with runtime checks). As a result, dynamic mode beats eager on some models, but on average is slower than eager due to three issues that are difficult to resolve fully. Constant folding and CSE limitations. Because shapes and strides are not constants during kernel generation, expressions that depend on them cannot be constant-folded or CSE’d. All address computations must therefore use integer division or modulo, which is expensive on the GPU; comparing kernels generated from the same subgraph in both modes, dynamic kernels are slower than their static counterparts. Vectorization path selection. The dynamic-shape kernel generator can guard only a single vector length at runtime, but TorchVision models require different optimal widths, so the vectorised path often does not trigger. Adding runtime checks for multiple widths (1, 2, 4, 8) would add overhead; vectorisation typically improves single-kernel performance by 20–25%. Layout propagation. For convolutional networks, layout propagation is an important optimisation. PyTorch’s default layout is row-major (NCHW), but convolution kernels are generally faster with NHWC layout because it better leverages tensor cores. Deep-learning compilers typically insert layout conversions at the network boundaries and keep intermediate tensors in NHWC. In dynamic mode all dimensions are unknown at compile time, so we cannot determine whether a tensor is NCHW or NHWC and cannot apply layout optimisation. Future work. Several improvements could alleviate these limitations. In practice not all dimensions are unknown—if most are statically known and only a few are dynamic, we could constant-fold more expressions during kernel generation. We could also build layout expressions parameterised by shape dimension variables, deriving the layout (NCHW vs. NHWC) at compile time and re-enabling layout optimisation. sections.heading: 5.2. Compilation cost
sections.text: Figure 3 compares compilation time for DLCB-static and DLCB-dynamic across the TorchVision suite. Both DLCB-static and DLCB-dynamic compile significantly faster than torch.compile , with a median compile time of 0.84 s versus 9.4 s for torch.compile — roughly a 10\times reduction (Figure 3 ). Crucially, the DLCB-dynamic compilation cost is an ahead-of-time overhead incurred once at model load; unlike torch.compile , no recompilation is triggered at runtime when new shapes are encountered.

sections.heading: 7. Conclusion
sections.text: We have presented DLCB, a deep learning compiler that resolves the tension between ahead-of-time compilation and dynamic tensor shapes through a constraint-based approach. For the common case in which tensor rank is statically known, DLCB generates CUDA kernels once, ahead of time, that execute correctly across a range of shapes by receiving dynamic dimensions as arguments at launch time. A constraint solver partitions dimensions into compile-time constants and runtime parameters, and compiles residual constraints into a compact host program that runs on the CPU before each kernel launch to verify shape invariants and supply the required arguments. When AOT compilation is not possible—because rank itself is unknown—the system falls back transparently to JIT compilation, providing a unified interface that always produces a runnable artifact. A key practical contribution is the automatic shape generalization pass in pytorch-dlcb. Users need not annotate their programs with symbolic dimensions: the pass identifies which dimensions are safe to abstract within a statically traced PyTorch program and generates the corresponding parameterised kernels automatically, lowering the barrier to deploying AOT-compiled kernels in production settings where input shapes vary. Our evaluation shows that DLCB’s dynamic-shape kernels approach fully-static compilation performance, demonstrating that the overhead of parameterising kernels by runtime dimensions is small in practice. A single dynamic binary also eliminates the repeated compilation cost that static approaches incur as input shapes vary across a deployment lifetime.
